rules.quote: Cite works of art using the author–date system.
rules.violation_condition: Works of art are cited using a referencing system other than author–date.
when: When citing works of art.
rules.why: G-4: retain the explicit instruction rather than the later description of the examples' referencing system.

covers.quote: This includes images and works of art.
Attribute artwork with correct references to help people find the source and relevant information.
copyright and permission information, if necessary.

rules.quote: You must attribute copyright material you reference.
rules.violation_condition: Referenced copyright artwork has no attribution, or an artwork image caption omits necessary copyright or permission information.
when: The referenced material is protected by copyright.
For artwork image captions, include copyright and permission information when necessary.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate the general attribution instruction and its explicit artwork-caption application.

rules.quote: Include all the details required by open access licences
rules.violation_condition: An attribution for openly licensed artwork omits licence-required details beyond the general artwork credit.
when: The artwork is used under an open access licence.
Determine the required details from the applicable licence.
rules.why: G-1: licence-specific attribution details are a distinct check from the general requirement to credit copyright material.

covers.quote: When including images of art in content, ensure they:

rules.quote: include alt text so that descriptions of the image can be read by screen readers or mobile users wishing to limit data usage.
rules.violation_condition: An image of an artwork has no descriptive alt text.
when: When including an image of art in content.
rules.why: G-1: retain the text-alternative requirement separately from the non-text image-display requirements.

rules.quote: Prepare short alt text for images
rules.specification: The page gives no word or character limit for 'short'. A reviewer must establish an operational interpretation before a length-based check is implemented.
rules.violation_condition: An artwork image's alt text is not short.
when: When providing alt text for an artwork image.
rules.why: G-1 and E-4: brevity is distinct from alt-text presence; do not invent a length threshold.

rules.quote: describe the relevant features of the work of art in the discussion to explain the relevance of the image.
rules.specification: Assess whether the discussion connects relevant features of the artwork to the reason for including the image; an exhaustive visual description is not required.
rules.violation_condition: The discussion accompanying an artwork image does not describe the features needed to explain the image's relevance.
when: When including an artwork image in content.
rules.why: G-1: explanatory discussion is a separate textual property from the presence and length of alt text.

covers.quote: Italicise the informal names of artworks in the same way that you would with the formal titles.
Write ‘Untitled’ in italics with an initial capital letter.
Write the titles of series of unique works of art in italics.
Write the titles of the individual works of art in the series in italics, too.
For example, write the title as the artist has and use italics for published works.

examples.note: The supplied blocks do not preserve the example's italic styling.

parts.quote: Margaret Olley’s Portrait in the mirror is one of her notable works. Portrait is usually included in retrospectives of Olley’s work.

examples.note: The supplied blocks do not preserve the example's italic styling.

parts.quote: Jackson Pollock titled his 1952 work Number 11 before it became known as Blue poles in a 1954 exhibition.

examples.note: The supplied blocks do not preserve the example's italic styling.

parts.quote: The exhibition included Coffin with flowers and potter’s wheel with landscape decoration, a drawing in the Potter series by Arthur Boyd.

rules.quote: Italicise the titles of individual artworks
rules.violation_condition: An individual artwork title, informal artwork name, untitled-work designation or artwork-series title is presented without italics.
when: Applies to formal and informal names of artworks.
Applies to ‘Untitled’ for a work with that title or no title.
Applies to titles of series of unique artworks and to the individual works in those series.
A sensible shortened title may be used from the second mention; it remains a title.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: these are applications of the same italicisation check, not separate rules for each artwork category.

covers.quote: Sometimes the artist has made a different typographic choice for the title. If so, follow the capitalisation of the original.
Write ‘Untitled’ in italics with an initial capital letter.
Use title case (maximal capitalisation).
Capitalise and punctuate according to the original title.
Modern works in a series might not use capital letters at all.

examples.note: This illustrates retaining an artist's capitalisation.

parts.quote: Parliament’s forecourt mosaic is based on Michael Nelson Jagamara’s Possum and Wallaby Dreaming.

examples.note: This contrasts series title case with an individual artwork title.

parts.quote: Sidney Nolan’s Ned Kelly series is currently touring Australia. Ned’s sister Margaret features in one of the works, Quilting the armour, painted in 1947.

examples.note: The lower-case individual title follows the original.

parts.quote: flight research #6 is part of Rosemary Laing’s Flight Research series.

rules.quote: use sentence case.
rules.violation_condition: An individual artwork title has capitalisation inconsistent with sentence case or the artist's differing original capitalisation; an artwork-series title is not in title case; or ‘Untitled’ lacks its initial capital.
when: Use sentence case for individual artwork titles unless the artist made a different capitalisation choice.
Preserve the artist's original capitalisation when it differs, including an entirely lower-case title.
Use title case for titles of series of unique artworks.
Write the designation ‘Untitled’ with an initial capital.
rules.why: G-2: title type and the artist's original choices change the applicable capitalisation, not the kind of error.

covers.quote: Capitalise and punctuate according to the original title.
From the second mention, you can use a shortened version of the name if it makes sense.

examples.note: The number and punctuation are part of the title.

parts.quote: William Yaxley used mandarin peel in his sculpture, The mangrove monster no. 2.

examples.note: The symbol and number are retained in the title.

parts.quote: flight research #6 is part of Rosemary Laing’s Flight Research series.

rules.quote: Include any numbers or punctuation in exactly the same way as the artist does.
rules.violation_condition: Numbers or punctuation in an artwork title differ from those in the artist's title.
when: Applies to individual artworks, including works in a series.
From the second mention, a shortened title is permitted if it makes sense; do not treat permitted shortening itself as a transcription error.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: consolidate title-punctuation fidelity across individual works; retain shortening as an exception.

covers.quote: Use the exact spelling.
You can include the English translation of the title.

examples.note: The original title is retained and an English translation accompanies it.

parts.quote: Bessie Davidson's Fleurs (flowers), completed in 1942, was sold in 2017.

rules.quote: If the title is in another language, write it in that language.
rules.violation_condition: A foreign-language artwork title is replaced by a translation or its original-language words are misspelt.
when: The artwork's title is in another language.
An English translation may accompany the original title.
From the second mention, a shortened version is permitted if it makes sense.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: original-language spelling is one fidelity check; an accompanying translation is permitted, not required.

covers.quote: Include the year of production and the artist’s name.
You might not be able to find the year of production. In this case, include the artist’s name and the medium of the work in square brackets.

examples.note: The artist and production year identify the untitled work.

parts.quote: Hunter’s Untitled (1968) is part of the permanent collection in the Museum of Contemporary Art.

examples.note: The bracketed medium is used when the production year is unavailable.

parts.quote: Dinh’s Untitled [oil on hardboard] was recently purchased for a private collection.

rules.quote: Write ‘Untitled’
rules.violation_condition: An untitled work is not identified as ‘Untitled’ with the artist and production year, or, when the year cannot be found, with the artist and a medium in square brackets.
when: The artist called the work ‘Untitled’ or gave it no name.
Include the production year and artist's name.
If the production year cannot be found, include the artist's name and the work's medium in square brackets.
The artist's name may be supplied in the surrounding sentence.
rules.why: G-2: year-known and year-unknown forms are conditional variants of the same untitled-work identification check; typography is handled separately.

examples.note: The example distinguishes the artwork's name from its earlier name.

parts.quote: Wrapped Coast, One Million Square Feet, Little Bay, Sydney, Australia was a work undertaken by artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude in 1968 and 1969. They used erosion-control fabric and polypropylene rope to wrap the coastline of Little Bay, where it remained for 10 weeks. Originally calledPacked Coast, sale of preparatory drawings funded the project.

rules.quote: Use the artwork’s correct name in use at a particular time.
rules.violation_condition: Ephemeral or performance artwork is identified by a name that was not correct for the time being discussed.
when: When citing ephemeral or performance art.
rules.why: G-1: historically correct naming is independently checkable and distinct from title formatting and contextual description.

covers.quote: It’s important to include detailed information because:

examples.note: The description supplies artists, dates, materials, location and duration.

parts.quote: Wrapped Coast, One Million Square Feet, Little Bay, Sydney, Australia was a work undertaken by artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude in 1968 and 1969. They used erosion-control fabric and polypropylene rope to wrap the coastline of Little Bay, where it remained for 10 weeks. Originally calledPacked Coast, sale of preparatory drawings funded the project.

rules.quote: Include context and details about the artwork to help people understand the work.
rules.specification: The page does not prescribe mandatory contextual facts or a sufficiency threshold. Adequacy depends on the artwork and the audience.
rules.violation_condition: A discussion of ephemeral or performance artwork lacks the contextual details needed to understand the work.
when: When citing ephemeral or performance art.
rules.why: G-4: the later explanation reinforces the contextual-detail requirement rather than creating another rule.

covers.quote: Write the titles of exhibitions in roman type

examples.note: The supplied blocks do not preserve the artwork/exhibition type-style contrast.

parts.quote: Cai Guo-Qiang’s Heritage(2013) is part of GOMA’s Water exhibition.

examples.note: The exhibition title is presented in roman type.

parts.quote: The Asia Pacific Triennial attracts visitors from all over Australia.

rules.quote: Use roman type for exhibition titles
rules.violation_condition: An exhibition title is set in italics rather than roman type.
when: The title names an exhibition, not its catalogue or an individual artwork.
rules.why: G-4: use the actionable heading and absorb its body restatement.

examples.note: The title retains the exhibition's capitalisation.

parts.quote: The Asia Pacific Triennial attracts visitors from all over Australia.

rules.quote: use the same capitalisation as the museum or gallery uses.
rules.violation_condition: An exhibition title's capitalisation differs from the museum's or gallery's form.
when: When writing the title of an exhibition.
rules.why: G-1: source capitalisation and roman type are independent properties and can fail separately.

covers.quote: Write catalogue titles in italics

examples.note: The supplied blocks do not preserve the catalogue title's italic styling.

parts.quote: The Philip Bacon Galleries produced a catalogue named Important Australian paintings.It accompanied the 2011 exhibition of the same name.

rules.quote: Use italics for titles of exhibition catalogues
rules.violation_condition: An exhibition-catalogue title is not italicised.
when: The title names an exhibition catalogue rather than the exhibition.
rules.why: G-4: retain the heading's italicisation check and absorb the matching body wording.

examples.note: The catalogue title uses sentence case, unlike the exhibition name identified in the gloss.

parts.quote: The Philip Bacon Galleries produced a catalogue named Important Australian paintings.It accompanied the 2011 exhibition of the same name.

rules.quote: use sentence case for the title.
rules.violation_condition: An exhibition-catalogue title is written in a case other than sentence case.
when: When writing an exhibition-catalogue title.
rules.why: G-1: catalogue-title capitalisation is independent of italicisation.

covers.quote: Include the name of the exhibition and the format of the catalogue in the reference list.
After the title of the exhibition, include the full start and end dates for the exhibition.
include an accessed date.
If you can’t link to a host page, include ‘PDF’ in square brackets after the format information.
Rule: Author or Gallery Name (Year) Title of exhibition [format] [PDF], Day Month Year of exhibition, Publisher, Place, accessed Day Month Year.

examples.note: Printed catalogue reference.

parts.quote: Philip Bacon Gallery (2011) Important Australian paintings [printed exhibition catalogue], 31 May to 25 June 2011, Philip Bacon Galleries, Brisbane.

examples.note: Online catalogue reference.

parts.quote: Campbell H (2010) Colour, rhythm, design: wood & lino cuts of the 20s and 30s [online exhibition catalogue], 13 March to 11 July 2010, Art Gallery of NSW, Sydney, accessed 23 February 2020.

rules.quote: Rule: Author or Gallery Name (Year) Title of exhibition [format], Day Month Year of exhibition, Publisher, Location of Gallery.
rules.violation_condition: An exhibition-catalogue reference has an incomplete or incorrectly arranged bibliographic structure, lacks the exhibition's full date range, or lacks an applicable online accessed date or PDF marker.
when: For exhibition-catalogue reference-list entries.
Include the exhibition name and catalogue format.
After the title, include the exhibition's full start and end dates.
For online catalogues, include an accessed date.
For a PDF that cannot be linked through a host page, put ‘PDF’ in square brackets after the format information.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: printed, online and directly linked PDF entries are conditional forms of one catalogue-reference structure.

covers.quote: If the catalogue is a PDF, link to the page where the PDF is hosted, instead of to the PDF.

rules.quote: For online catalogues, hyperlink the title of the catalogue
rules.violation_condition: An online catalogue's title is not hyperlinked, or a PDF catalogue is linked directly when a host page can be linked instead.
when: For online catalogues.
For a PDF catalogue, link the title to the page hosting the PDF rather than directly to the file.
If a host page cannot be linked, the reference must identify the PDF as specified by the catalogue-reference rule.
rules.why: G-2: the PDF condition changes the correct destination of the same catalogue-title link.

rules.quote: Use common abbreviations where possible
rules.specification: The page supplies neither an abbreviation inventory nor a test for 'where possible'. These need to be agreed before this can become a reliable check.
rules.violation_condition: Artwork details use an expanded or nonstandard form where a suitable common abbreviation is available.
when: When presenting artwork details in publications or captions.
rules.why: G-1: abbreviation choice is a textual requirement separate from consistency across a publication.

rules.quote: be consistent.
rules.specification: Interpret this local instruction as consistency in abbreviation use for artwork details. The separately stated long-versus-short caption-style requirement is checked independently.
rules.violation_condition: Equivalent artwork details use inconsistent abbreviation forms within the same publication without a contextual reason.
when: When presenting artwork details in one publication.
rules.why: G-1: inconsistent abbreviation use is different from choosing a nonstandard abbreviation or mixing long and short caption styles.

covers.quote: the full details of the work of art
Rule: Creator Full Name (Year) Title or description of work [medium], Website, Exhibition or Gallery, Location of Gallery, © Creator, courtesy: Creator or Gallery, accessed Date Month Year.

examples.note: Artwork-image caption.

parts.quote: Megan Cope (1982) Quandamooka people[hand-cast concrete oyster shells, copper slag, foam support structure], RE FORMATION 2019, Australia, © and image courtesy: Megan Cope.

examples.note: Artwork-image caption.

parts.quote: Angela Tiatia (2015) Holding on[still], Sullivan + Strumpf Gallery, Sydney, © Angela Tiatia, courtesy: Sullivan + Strumpf Gallery.

rules.quote: If your content features an image of an artwork, it must accompanied by a caption with:
rules.specification: Use the supplied caption template to identify applicable work details. The examples omit some template fields, so do not require a website or accessed date for every caption regardless of source. Copyright and permission information is covered by the attribution rule.
rules.violation_condition: An artwork image in digital content lacks a caption containing the applicable details identifying the work.
when: The content is digital and features an image of an artwork.
Include applicable creator, year, title or description, medium, source or venue, and location details.
Include online-source and access information where applicable.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: the lead-in, required work details and template form one image-caption requirement; rights information is consolidated with attribution.

rules.quote: For each collection, exhibition or catalogue, use either a long or short caption style and use that style consistently.
rules.violation_condition: A collection, exhibition or catalogue mixes long and short artwork-caption styles.
when: Assess consistency within each collection, exhibition or catalogue.
rules.why: G-1: consistency across captions is distinct from the field order within an individual caption.

rules.quote: If it’s a solo exhibition, don’t include the artist’s name on each artwork.
